segments.say: Lesson 20. Design Video Streaming (YouTube). Upload pipeline, transcoding D A G, adaptive bitrate streaming (H L S/D A S H), C D N and metadata.

Design a video platform like YouTube: creators upload large videos, which are converted into many formats, and viewers worldwide stream them smoothly at the right quality. Here is an analogy. A film distributor: receive the master reel, make copies in every format (cinema, T V, phone), and store copies in warehouses near every city.

Why does this matter? Covers large file uploads, background processing pipelines and C D Ns. A few key words. Transcoding: Converting video into different resolutions and formats. Segment: A short 2–10 second piece of video. Adaptive bitrate: Player switches quality as the network changes. Pre-signed U R L: Temporary permission to upload directly to storage.
Upload leads to process leads to stream. Creator uploads via a pre-signed U R L straight to blob storage, chunked and resumable, so huge files never pass through app servers.
Raw file lands in object storage. Metadata row status equals "processing".
An event triggers the transcoding pipeline (a D A G): split into chunks leads to encode in parallel into many resolutions and codecs leads to thumbnails, captions, content checks.
Output: small segments (2–10 s) per resolution plus a manifest (H L S.m3u8 / D A S H.mpd). Status leads to "ready".
Segments are served from a C D N. Popular videos get cached at edges near viewers; the long tail is served from origin.
Adaptive bitrate: the player measures bandwidth and picks the next segment's quality: 1080p on Wi-Fi, 360p on a weak 4G signal, without stopping.

Requirements & scale. Upload, transcode, stream smoothly worldwide. Search, comments, recommendations are secondary. Read-heavy (views ≫ uploads). Bandwidth is the dominant cost, so the C D N is the hero. Storage: each video is stored in multiple renditions, often 2–5 times the source size.

Deep dives. Transcoding at scale: split into G O P-aligned chunks, process in parallel on a worker fleet (or spot instances), coordinate via a D A G or workflow engine, retry failed chunks. Cost: encode popular videos in more formats (AV1/VP9) and the long tail in fewer. Move cold content to cheaper storage tiers. View counts: aggregated asynchronously (Kafka leads to stream processing), eventually consistent. Live streaming: similar segments but generated in real time, with lower latency targets.

Say it in the interview. "Uploads go directly to object storage via resumable pre-signed U R Ls. An event kicks off a parallel transcoding D A G that produces H L S/D A S H segments at multiple bitrates plus thumbnails. Metadata lives in a D B, segments are served through a C D N, and players use adaptive bitrate. Views and analytics are processed asynchronously.".

Let's compare. Large uploads: pre-signed U R Ls, chunked resumable upload. Many devices / networks: multiple renditions plus adaptive bitrate (H L S/D A S H). Global latency & bandwidth: C D N edge caching. Processing time: parallel chunked transcoding D A G. Storage cost: tiered storage, fewer renditions for cold videos. Counts & analytics: async stream processing.

A likely interview question: Design YouTube in 60 seconds. A strong answer: Pre-signed resumable uploads to blob storage, an event-driven parallel transcoding D A G producing H L S/D A S H renditions and thumbnails, metadata D B, C D N distribution with adaptive bitrate playback, async view counting and recommendations. Optimize egress and storage tiers for cost.
That's it for Design Video Streaming (YouTube). Now play the quiz and games in the app to lock it in. See you in the next lesson.
